evidence.source: Wang Ning, Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Ancient Chinese Characters
evidence.text: In this 2010 article, Wang reports oracle-bone uses of 白 for “white,” 伯, and a place name, surveys earlier proposals including a thumb, and argues instead that the graph depicts a cooking or measuring vessel. He treats the color word and 伯 as homophonic loans from that proposed graph. This is the author’s hypothesis, not an established consensus.
evidence.title: 王寧：再說“白”字之本義

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: reported early uses and competing thumb account
evidence.text: The search result reports a thumb interpretation attributed to Guo Moruo, connects the thumb’s supposed leading position with 伯, and says 白 was borrowed for the color word. It lists oracle-bone examples for 伯, white, and 百, including corpus identifiers. The page timed out when opened in this invocation, so these details are recorded as search-result leads, not independently inspected page evidence.

search_audit.outcome: The opened Fudan article reports oracle-bone use categories but does not establish their order or provide individually dated inscription contexts. The CUHK result offers corpus identifiers, but its page could not be opened.

search_audit.outcome: Search returned a result summarizing the CUHK account and examples. The direct page timed out when opened, so no additional claims from it are counted as inspected evidence.

gaps: The reviewed sources conflict about whether the early graph depicted a thumb or a vessel and about the direction of the relationship between 白 and 伯. The Fudan author proposes a vessel and treats both words as loans; the CUHK search result summarizes a thumb account in which 白 was used for 伯 and later for the color word. The available inspected page does not settle this direction, so omit a directed meaning-history development or describe the direction as unresolved.

The Fudan article reports oracle-bone uses for white, 伯, and a place name but gives no individually dated contexts that establish their relative order. CUHK search-result text lists corpus identifiers, but the direct page timed out; those examples were not verified here against primary facsimiles or dating evidence.

Wang Ning’s proposed vessel identification does not independently establish the vessel’s ancient name or pronunciation. The proposed phonetic loan cannot be confirmed from a reconstruction of 白 alone.

No new glyph-source inspection in this invocation requires changing the existing candidates. Existing glyphs are modern script-style redrawings, not verified photographs of dated artifacts; their selection and visual descriptions remain subject to the dossier’s downstream pixel inspection.
